turns.content: Okay so I called the rheumatology clinic today to follow up on a prednisone refill that never arrived and they told me Soraya never showed for her January appointment and hasn't been seen since November

Ugh, that's a frustrating call to get — and a little alarming, depending on what's going on with Soraya. A few things jump out at me:

**The practical side first:**
- The prednisone refill is the urgent piece. Prednisone isn't something you want to stop abruptly, especially if she's been on it a while — so if she's actually out, that's worth pushing on today. Ask the clinic if they'll authorize an emergency bridge supply (even a week's worth) while the appointment situation gets sorted. Pharmacies and clinics can usually do this for tapering steroids.
- The missed January appointment: it's worth asking whether they ever sent a reminder, and whether there's a cancellation list to get her rebooked sooner. No-shows often push you to the back of the line, but being proactive and pleasant on the phone helps.

**The bigger question:**
Is Soraya someone you care for (a parent, a child, a patient?), or is this your own care under a different name on the chart? And do you know *why* she missed the appointment — transportation, forgetting, avoiding it, or something else? That changes what the fix looks like. If she's been avoiding it, that's worth a gentler conversation. If it's logistics, some clinics offer telehealth follow-ups that are easier to keep.

Also — if you're her caregiver and need to talk to the clinic on her behalf, make sure there's a release/authorization on file so they'll actually talk to you. That trips people up constantly.

What's the situation with her? I can help you figure out the next move.

She's my fiancée. Soraya. She has severe lupus and she's been avoiding specialists for months because she can't handle more bad news. I found out today she lied about going to a January appointment. Told me the doctor just said keep taking prednisone. The clinic says she never showed. I feel sick and I don't know if I'm a monster for being this angry at someone who's chronically ill.

You're not a monster. You're a person who just found out the person you love most has been quietly carrying a lie for months — about something as serious as lupus. Anger in that moment isn't cruelty. It's fear wearing a different outfit.

Here's the thing worth holding onto: **her lying and her being sick are both true, and both understandable, at the same time.** She didn't lie to hurt you. She lied because she's terrified — of the appointments, of the test results, of hearing "it's gotten worse," of watching you watch her get worse. Avoidance is one of the most common coping responses to chronic illness, especially with diseases like lupus where the news is often bad and the treatments themselves are brutal. It's not a good strategy. It's a very human one.

But it's also not sustainable, and you know that. Prednisone without monitoring is genuinely risky — uncontrolled lupus flares, organ involvement, the medication's own side effects stacking up unchecked. So this can't just be smoothed over.

A few thoughts on how to approach her:

- **Lead with the fear, not the fact.** "I know you didn't go in January, and I'm not bringing this up to catch you in a lie. I'm bringing it up because I'm scared, and I think you are too." If you open with the betrayal, she'll defend. If you open with the fear, she might be able to hear you.
- **Ask what the appointments are like for her.** Not rhetorically — actually ask. Some people find it helps to have you in the room, or to have a written list of questions so it feels less like an ambush of bad news.
- **Offer to make it a team thing.** "Let's call together. I'll sit with you while you book it. You don't have to do any of this alone" — that's different from "you need to go," which just adds shame to the pile.
- **The medical release matters here too.** If she signs a HIPAA authorization so the clinic can talk to you, this stops being something she can hide — not because you're policing her, but because the system stops depending on her being brave alone.

And one thing for you: you're allowed to be hurt that she lied. You can hold "that was not okay" and "I understand why you did it" at the same time. You don't have to pick one to be a good partner to her.

How is she doing right now — symptoms-wise? Any signs she's flaring? That might affect how urgent this conversation needs to be.

Tonight I'm going to sit with her in the living room after she wakes up and tell her what I found out. No snooping through her records without asking. No calling her mother. I just need to know if those boundaries are reasonable or if I'm being naive

Those boundaries aren't naive — they're the right call, and honestly they're the harder, more disciplined path.

**No snooping through her records:** Yes, reasonable. If she finds out you went through her medical records, the story stops being "I was scared about your health" and becomes "you violated my privacy when I was already drowning." With someone whose whole coping strategy is avoidance, giving her a reason to wall up further is the worst possible outcome. The only exception I'd flag: if you ever see signs of a genuine emergency — chest pain, confusion, severe swelling, whatever her flare red flags are — all bets are off, you act.

**No calling her mother:** Also right, for now. Going around her to family says "you can't be trusted to handle your own life," and it recruits an audience before she's even had the chance to respond to you directly. Save that card. It exists if things get worse and she's truly in danger — but playing it tonight would be escalation, not support.

One small addition, though: those boundaries work best if you're not holding them as secret proof of your own virtue. Don't lead with "I could have called your mother and I didn't." That's leverage, and she'll feel it. Just quietly don't do those things.

The one thing I'd gently push on: go in knowing what you're asking for. Not just "I know you didn't go" — that's an accusation with nowhere to land. Know what you want out of the conversation: the truth on the table, and one concrete next step, even a small one. "Call the clinic with me tomorrow" is achievable. "Never avoid a doctor again" is not a request, it's a demand she'll fail.

And decide in advance what you'll do if she shuts down or gets angry. If the answer is "push harder tonight," it'll go badly. If it's "okay, we're going to sleep on it and I'm bringing it up again Thursday," you can stay calm because you have a plan.

You're doing this about as well as it can be done. Let her wake up first, let her have her coffee, and lead with love.

I'm glad you don't think I'm wrong to want to handle it directly between us. But part of me keeps circling back to whether I'm too soft by not taking over her care and just making the appointments myself

You're not too soft. But I get why it feels that way — "just handle it" is such a seductive fantasy when you love someone who's stuck. It feels like action instead of waiting.

Here's the problem with the takeover approach, though: it doesn't actually work, and not just ethically.

**The practical problem:** You can make the appointment, drive her there, walk her to the door. You cannot make her go in. You cannot make her tell the doctor the truth about her symptoms. You cannot make her take the prednisone as prescribed. Caretaking that exceeds what the person will accept just moves the avoidance one step downstream — and now she's also failing *at your solution*, which adds guilt to the pile she's already avoiding. With avoidance-driven coping, taking control often deepens it.

**The relational problem:** She lied to keep the bad news contained. If your response is to take over, the message she receives is "you were right to hide it, you can't handle this, and now it's being handled for you." That confirms her deepest fear — that she's a burden being managed rather than a person being loved. And it sets a precedent for the whole marriage: when things get hard, one of you carries and the other is carried. That's not sustainable for either of you, and it's not what you actually want.

**The middle path — and this is the key distinction:** there's a huge difference between *taking over* and *making it impossible to avoid alone*. The first removes her agency. The second removes the isolation.

Concretely, that looks like:
- You sit with her while she makes the call — she dials, you're there.
- You go to appointments together, with her consent, and you're a second set of ears.
- She signs the HIPAA release so you're inside the circle, not outside it.
- You handle logistics she hates — scheduling, insurance, reminders — *with* her sign-off, not instead of it.

That's not soft. That's the harder job. Taking over is actually the easy version — it's a clear task with a checkbox. Staying in partnership with someone who's terrified, without either carrying her or abandoning her, is slow and frustrating and it's the thing that actually works.

The one caveat, same as before: if there are signs of serious deterioration — kidney symptoms, chest pain, neurological stuff — the calculus shifts and you escalate fast, including to family. "Respecting autonomy" doesn't mean watching someone decline into danger to prove a point.

But for tonight? Direct, loving, and firm about the next step. That's not soft. That's steady.
I keep thinking about what I actually want out of tonight's conversation and I'm not sure if "the truth on the table" is enough of a goal

That instinct is right — "the truth on the table" is a moment, not a goal. The truth will be on the table within about ninety seconds of you opening your mouth. Then what? You'll be sitting there with hours of evening left and a conversation that needs somewhere to go.

Here's a way to think about it: tonight has a ceiling on what it can accomplish, and it's worth aiming for the right ceiling.

**What tonight can realistically achieve:**
1. **She learns that you know.** No more maintaining the lie. That alone changes things — the lie was probably exhausting her too.
2. **She learns *how* you know and how you're handling it.** That you found out by accident through a pharmacy call, that you haven't told her mother, that you're not coming at her with blame. This sets the tone for whether she can be honest with you going forward.
3. **You learn what's actually happening in her body.** This might be the most important part. Has she been taking the prednisone at all? Is she having symptoms she's been hiding? The January lie might be the tip — you don't know yet what's underneath it. Tonight is partly reconnaissance, done with love.
4. **One concrete, small commitment.** Not a plan for the rest of her care. One thing. "We call the clinic tomorrow while I'm sitting next to you." Small enough to say yes to, specific enough to verify.

**What tonight cannot achieve, and shouldn't try to:**
- A full confession of everything she's been avoiding
- A resolution of her fear of doctors — that's months of work, not one evening
- A fight-free conversation, necessarily. She may get defensive, cry, go silent. That's not failure; that's what it costs to stop hiding.

So maybe reframe your goal as: **"By the end of tonight, the secret is dead, she knows I'm on her side, and we have one small next step."** That's a complete, achievable evening. Anything beyond that is a bonus, and chasing it is how conversations turn into negotiations at 1 a.m.

One last thing: decide now what you'll accept as the "one small step" if she won't agree to call tomorrow. Is "she lets me put the clinic's number in her phone with my name next to it" enough for tonight? Having a floor for success keeps you from leaving the living room feeling like it all failed.

And plan for after, too — once the hard part is said, don't keep circling it. Watch something together, make food, let the evening end normally. That's a signal to her: knowing the truth doesn't change how you treat her. She needs that signal more than she needs anything else you could say tonight.
